docs.title: SQL Injection (SQLi)
docs.text: Improper neutralization of special elements used in an SQL command allows attacker-controlled data to alter the query structure (G78/Owasp). Successful exploitation can disclose, modify, or destroy database data and may lead to full application compromise.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database access; never concatenate user input into SQL. Apply least-privilege database accounts, validate input against strict allow-lists, and use an ORM with safe bindings where practical.

sections.heading: Detection
sections.text: Look for string-built queries (f-strings, + concatenation, format()) feeding cursor.execute, raw query planners, and error messages that echo SQL syntax back to the client.

docs.title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
docs.text: A password, API key, or other secret is baked into source code. Anyone with repository access (or anyone who obtains a copy) can authenticate as the trusted component, and rotation requires a code change.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Move secrets to environment variables or a secret manager, rotate any exposed credential immediately, and scan history for prior leaks. Commit pre-receive hooks with detect-secrets/gitleaks prevent regressions.

docs.title: Cross-site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text: Web applications include untrusted data in output pages without proper validation or escaping, allowing attackers to execute scripts in victims' browsers (session hijacking, defacement, credential theft).

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Context-escape all dynamic output (HTML, JS, URL, CSS contexts), prefer framework auto-escaping and safe DOM APIs (textContent over innerHTML), sanitize rich HTML with a vetted allow-list sanitizer, and deploy a restrictive Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: OS Command Injection
docs.text: User-controlled data reaches an OS shell command, letting attackers execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges (RCE).

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Avoid shells: use argument-array APIs (subprocess.run([...]) with shell=False), validate input against strict allow-lists, and drop privileges for child processes.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text: External input is used to construct a path that can escape the intended directory, exposing or overwriting arbitrary files (source disclosure, config theft, code execution via writable paths).

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Resolve the final path with os.path.realpath/Path.resolve and verify it stays under the intended root; prefer id-based access over user paths; block ../ and absolute paths; run with least filesystem privilege.

docs.title: Exposure of Sensitive Information
docs.text: The application leaks confidential data (PII, secrets, internal state, stack traces) to actors not authorized to see it, via responses, logs, error pages, or side channels.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Minimize data returned, redact secrets and PII in responses and logs, disable debug error pages in production, and enforce server-side authorization on every object.

docs.title: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
docs.text: Sensitive data travels in cleartext (HTTP, FTP, unencrypted SMTP), allowing network observers to capture credentials, tokens, and personal data.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Enforce HTTPS/TLS everywhere with HSTS, disable plaintext fallbacks, and use encrypted protocols (SMTPS/IMAPS) for mail.

docs.title: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
docs.text: A sensitive operation (account admin, payment, config change) is reachable without proving identity, letting any attacker invoke it directly.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Require authentication on every critical route by default (deny-by-default), enforce authorization checks server-side, and add regression tests that unauthenticated requests are rejected with 401/403.

docs.title: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (IDOR)
docs.text: Objects are accessed by directly guessing or manipulating an identifier (id, uuid, account number) without verifying the caller owns or may access that object.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Enforce object-level authorization on every access (ownership/tenant checks server-side), prefer non-guessable identifiers, and never trust IDs from the client without a permission lookup.

docs.title: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
docs.text: Parsing attacker-controlled serialized objects (pickle, yaml.load, Java serialization) can trigger gadget chains that execute arbitrary code or instantiate attacker-chosen types.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Never deserialize untrusted data with unsafe formats; use JSON for untrusted payloads, safe loaders (yaml.safe_load), and integrity-check signed payloads before parsing.

docs.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
docs.text: The server fetches a user-supplied URL, letting attackers reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), or scan the private network from the server's vantage point.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Allow-list outbound destinations, resolve and validate IPs (block private/link-local ranges), disable redirects, and separate egress networks for user-initiated fetches.

docs.title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits
docs.text: Unbounded allocation of files, memory, connections, or compute per request lets an attacker exhaust resources and cause denial of service for all users.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Apply quotas and rate limits per user/IP, bound request body and collection sizes, and set timeouts on all outbound calls.

docs.title: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
docs.text: Use of broken or weak algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 for signatures, DES, ECB mode) undermines confidentiality or integrity guarantees even when crypto is 'used'.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Use modern algorithms (AES-GCM, SHA-256+, ChaCha20-Poly1305), prefer vetted libraries and authenticated encryption, and never design your own crypto.

docs.title: Use of Insufficiently Random Values
docs.text: Predictable random values (math.random for tokens, time-based seeds) allow attackers to guess session tokens, password-reset links, or nonces.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Use cryptographically secure generators (secrets, os.urandom, crypto/rand) for all security-sensitive values, and never seed PRNGs with time or low-entropy input.

docs.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Reference
docs.text: XML parsers that resolve external entities let attackers read local files, perform SSRF, or exhaust resources while parsing seemingly benign XML.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Disable DTDs and external entity resolution in all XML parsers; prefer JSON for untrusted data.

docs.title: Improper Handling of Syntax Errors (input validation)
docs.text: Unhandled malformed input causes crashes or inconsistent state instead of clean rejection, enabling denial of service and masking of real attacks in noisy errors.

sections.heading: Remediation
sections.text: Validate all external input against schemas, reject malformed data with clear 4xx responses, and fail closed without leaking internals.
